narrative:
The model estimates an 85% chance that you will leave your job in the near future. In this decision, that high predicted probability is the reason you were denied a promotion at this time; it is not a judgment of your ability.

The strongest signal driving this prediction is your total years of work experience. At 6–10 years, you are more experienced than the largest group of colleagues predicted to stay, most of whom have only 1–5 years overall, and this profile pushed the prediction toward leaving. The second strongest signal is your tenure in your current organization: having 1–5 years here also pushed the prediction toward leaving. The third is that you have received other job opportunities while in this role; only about one in four employees predicted to stay reported such opportunities, so this strongly raised the leaving risk.

Taken together, the model sees an experienced employee with relatively short current tenure and visible outside options as likely to move. To revisit promotion eligibility, you and your manager should discuss concrete retention and growth steps: internal career paths, a clear promotion timeline, development opportunities, and how to address the pull of external offers. The organization should also check whether workload, recognition, pay satisfaction, stability, or support need attention, since those can reinforce a decision to stay.
